fields.Front: What does a sequence diagram show, and what does it complement?
fields.Back: The flow of messages (method calls) between objects during a particular scenario or use case, modelling interactions over time as a sequence of events. It complements use case diagrams by capturing dynamic behaviour: a class diagram shows static structure, a sequence diagram shows what happens at run time.

fields.Front: List the four elements of a sequence diagram and how each is drawn.
fields.Back: Actors: external entities, stick figures at the top. Objects/participants: boxes at the top with a dashed vertical lifeline below each. Messages: arrows between lifelines (solid for a call, dashed for a return). Conditions: control-flow frames such as alt and loops.

fields.Front: What is an alt fragment, and how is it read?
fields.Back: A labelled frame around a region, divided by dashed lines into guarded regions each with a condition in square brackets, e.g. [If card is valid]. Exactly one region executes. Frames can be nested inside one another.

fields.Front: Trace the opening of the ATM sequence diagram, up to the first alt.
fields.Back: User -> ATM: Insert Card. ATM -> BankServer: Verify Card. Then the outer alt opens on [If card is valid], in which BankServer replies Card OK (dashed) to ATM.

fields.Front: Inside [If card is valid] and [If PIN is valid], what messages lead up to the funds check?
fields.Back: ATM -> User: Request PIN; User -> ATM: PIN Entered; ATM -> BankServer: Verify PIN; BankServer replies PIN OK; ATM -> User: Request Amount; User -> ATM: Amount Entered; ATM -> BankServer: Start Transaction; BankServer -> BankAccount: Sufficient Funds?

fields.Front: What happens in the ATM diagram when funds are sufficient?
fields.Back: BankAccount -> BankServer: Funds OK; BankServer -> ATM: Withdraw Amount; ATM -> User: Dispense Cash; and Transaction Successful returns from BankServer to ATM.

fields.Front: What happens in the [Insufficient funds] region of the ATM diagram?
fields.Back: BankAccount -> BankServer: Insufficient Funds; BankServer -> ATM: Transaction Unsuccessful; ATM -> User: Eject Card.

fields.Front: What happens in the [PIN Invalid] and [Card Invalid] regions?
fields.Back: [PIN Invalid]: BankServer replies PIN Invalid and the ATM sends Eject Card. [Card Invalid]: BankServer replies Card Invalid and the ATM sends Eject Card. Both failure paths return the card without dispensing cash.

fields.Front: Which of the five kinds of object response does the ATM diagram make visible?
fields.Back: BankAccount returns a value from its state (Funds OK); BankServer delegates to BankAccount; the ATM updates state and forwards. The whole flow is a chain of messages between objects that each own one responsibility.

fields.Text: In a sequence diagram time flows {{c1::downward}}, a {{c1::solid}} arrow is a call, and a {{c1::dashed}} arrow is a return or reply.
The ATM sequence diagram has four participants across the top: the actor {{c1::User}}, and the objects {{c1::ATM}}, {{c1::BankServer}}, and {{c1::BankAccount}}.
The ATM diagram's three nested alt guards, outer to inner: [If {{c1::card is valid}}], [If {{c1::PIN is valid}}], [If {{c1::funds are sufficient}}].
fields.Extra: Their else regions are [Card Invalid], [PIN Invalid], and [Insufficient funds], and all three end with Eject Card.

fields.Text: Modelling guidance for sequence diagrams: {{c1::clarity over completeness}} and {{c1::iterative design}}; the named pitfalls are {{c1::too many classes}} and {{c1::making diagrams too detailed for the audience}}.
fields.Extra: A diagram should tell one scenario clearly, not every possible path; a stakeholder review needs less detail than an implementation handoff.

fields.Text: A sequence diagram shows {{c1::messages (method calls)}} between objects for one scenario, modelling {{c1::dynamic}} behaviour over time - whereas a class diagram shows {{c1::static structure}}.
